extracted.intended_audience: improvisational theatre performers, directors, coaches and students (stage/cabaret improv)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for choosing, running and practising short-form and theatrical improv games (audience-facing and workshop contexts), with notes on timing, safety, difficulty, and control dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caller selection and timing management
rubrics_metrics.description: The caller should be happy to cheat the times a little, rather than leave the improvisers hanging or cut them off—that’s why it may be inadvisable to give this role to an audience member who may delight in exposing the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a reliable caller (not an audience member likely to expose mistakes). The caller may bend strict timing to preserve flow and avoid awkward cut-offs; managing timings sympathetically is part of good calling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of caller-player relationship to structure iterations
rubrics_metrics.description: The relationship between the caller and the players can be exploited to give a little more appeal: the caller can be a little critical of the initial scene and request progressively shorter versions (e.g., 60s, 30s, 15s) to add structure and dramatic interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is contrived but useful occasionally (e.g., to boost a show or end strongly). Players may affect being put-out and then comply; useful for calming anxious improvisers by giving a mechanical exercise to succeed at.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mechanical/format games sparingly to calm anxious performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical games (highly structured, repetitive) are recommended for occasional use when a show needs a boost or a big finish; having made a mechanical game work will calm anxious improvisers and help them take risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve such games for particular situations (warm-up, finale, nervous casts); do not overuse them or let them become the default retreat from risk and storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid First Line/Last Line in ordinary public performance (risk of hesitancy and anticlimax)
rubrics_metrics.description: First Line/Last Line tends to generate hesitancy and bridging; endings must make sense yet be surprising, and the game often produces slow, joyless plods to an obvious endpoint or frantic, unconvincing slottings of the last line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The game is almost guaranteed to produce the wrong behavior for good storytelling and is likely to be an anticlimax; use with caution and consider alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: If using First Line/Last Line, turn it into a competition
rubrics_metrics.description: About the best way to play First Line/Last Line well is to make it a competition to see which pair can get from first line to last line in the shortest time or fewest lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnifying the importance of the game eliminates the attempt to tell a story within its confines (the 'nuclear option'); accept that this condemns the game to occasional use for variety rather than regular storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endowment games generally poor for storytelling; avoid for theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: Endowment/Interrogation Endowment forces one player to guess hidden information and typically prevents any kind of story from emerging; scenes degenerate into a procession of clues and usually outstay their welcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endowment games often produce blocking, repetitive guessing, and audience relief rather than engagement; they’re not recommended for improvised theatre or cabaret unless reworked carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: When playing Endowment-like games, set limits and design for theatre
rubrics_metrics.description: If you must play endowment games, strategies include: time-limiting the game, prioritizing funny clues over obscure ones, ending immediately when solved, using structured Master/Servant variants to create legitimate conflict, or embedding the guessing as an incidental feature of a real scene (e.g., aligning the absent player's emotional state with the secret).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tips: ~90 seconds for three clues; don’t force recaps; use extra improvisers as ‘Constable Obvious’ sparingly; integrate the secret into character psychology so guessing becomes a dramatic device rather than the scene's sole focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep 'freak show' spectacle games short and safe
rubrics_metrics.description: Freak-show games (Bucket of Death, Mousetrap Game) focus audience interest on spectacle rather than story; they must be brief and safety-conscious (e.g., keep the bucket water lukewarm; do not use rat traps; have spotters for blindfolded players).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit duration to avoid audience habituation; prioritize performer safety (no real dangerous traps), and accept that story content will be secondary to the stunt—use such games only sparingly and for special occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose games that look hard but are easier than they appear
rubrics_metrics.description: Games which appear difficult to an audience but are generally easier for players are valuable: the audience enjoys perceived risk while still seeing success (e.g., Alphabet). Conversely, avoid games that look easy but are actually hard for your players in public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a group's strengths: if a game confuses a significant fraction of players, do not play it in public. Use 'easier-than-they-look' games as quick wins that still allow storytelling; tough games are worth preserving for practice until you reach comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice rhyming carefully; respect rhythm and stress
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhyming improvisation fails mainly because performers panic and ignore the pattern of vocal stress; rhythm determines what the audience expects to rhyme, so focus on stress and cadence rather than forcing immediate rhymes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop an ear by reading poetry aloud (e.g., Dr. Seuss, Poe) and practising rhythm; only perform sustained rhyming in public when you are reliably competent, because audience frustration at errors is immediately obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use singing and music selectively and with appropriate skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvised singing can lift an audience hugely, but improvising both melody and lyrics well requires musical skill; mediocre improvised songs are relatively easy but can be overused as a crutch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the group has strong musical chops (musicians, varied styles, melody and lyric improvisation skills), musical improv can sustain long-form shows; otherwise, avoid over-reliance on songs that 'always work' as they reduce storytelling variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'always works'/safe options with suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: Anything you see as a safe option, anything which 'always works', should be confronted with deep suspicion and mistrust because over-praising something that always works can lead to repetition and a retreat from risk and storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversify formats and resist audience demands for the same repeatable bits; preserve storytelling by challenging the troupe with new risks rather than defaulting to safe crowd-pleasers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disliked games diagnostically and practise weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: If you dislike a particular game but suspect it might teach you something, that dislike reveals a weakness in your technique and is an opportunity: practice that game repeatedly (off-stage or in workshop) until the antipathy wanes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not avoid work that exposes weaknesses; treat it like a tennis player practising a weak serve—deliberate, repeated practice until competence is achieved, then consider public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop flexibility in control: practice taking and ceding control
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers differ in preference for control: 'Clevers' plan and push scenes forward, while 'Quiets' follow; the ideal improviser can both generate ideas and happily let a partner run the scene—learning to take and cede control is central to strong ensemble work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid only playing cooperation-balancing games; instead practise exercises that force one player to 'work' another and alternate roles so performers learn both leading and following. Address group imbalances (two Clevers or two Quiets) by training role flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Sandy Carroll and its variants to train control dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Sandy Carroll: one player restricted to four phrases ('Yes', 'Okay', 'Sounds good to me', 'I'll go along with that') while partner has full freedom. Variants include Negative Sandy Carroll (restricted to blocking phrases) and Diet Sandy Carroll (one lets partner lead but can add details until they would).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run these in pairs and as group exercises; use side-coaching to teach how to make a 'yes' create suffering, to learn to play vulnerability, and to force Clevers and Quiets out of habitual roles. Avoid Negative Sandy Carroll in ordinary practice (it generates blocking), but use Diet Sandy Carroll to teach restraint and led-follow dynamics.
